---
title: "Random intercept models"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

[Partial pooling](random-effects.qmd) gave each participant and word a fitted deviation from a shared population center. We now put one of those deviations inside a regression equation. A **random intercept** adds one group's deviation to the population intercept. It moves that group's entire fitted relation up or down while leaving the predictor coefficients unchanged.

Why do we need it? The [MALD incidence structure](structured-data.qmd) shows that several rows come from the same listener and several rows contain the same spoken word. A persistent listener difference enters every row from that listener, so the model should represent the shared source. We model the remaining intercept deviations with a normal population distribution, which assumes a symmetric, single-peaked distribution around zero after included predictors.

Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) applies after the shared intercepts are supplied. Integrating them induces [covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) among repeated responses, and the [residual](residuals.qmd) records what remains at the trial level. A fitted participant or item intercept summarizes repeated responses under MALD's task and restrictions.

We first insert one participant deviation and derive its covariance, then add crossed word variation, fit the model, and compare raw with conditionally fitted participant baselines.

## Inserting a participant deviation

For trial $i$ from participant $p$, a participant-intercept model has

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\mathbf x_{pi}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_{pi},
$$

with

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{pi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Participant $p$ has fitted baseline $\beta_0+b_p$. The deviation changes the vertical location of the participant's regression relation; it does not change any predictor association.

## Deriving the induced covariance

Two trials from the same participant share $b_p$:

$$
Y_{pi}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
\qquad
Y_{pi'}=\beta_0+b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'}.
$$

Under independent residuals and independence between residuals and the group deviation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{pi},Y_{pi'})
&=\operatorname{Cov}(b_p+\varepsilon_{pi},
                     b_p+\varepsilon_{pi'})\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[b_p]\\
&=\tau_p^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Conditional on $b_p$, the residuals may be independent. Marginally, before the deviation is known, the two responses are associated because they contain the same participant baseline.

The fitted variance components below let us calculate the size of this shared contribution in MALD. We derive and name the corresponding correlation next.

Every cancellation uses an assumption: different trial residuals are uncorrelated, residuals are uncorrelated with $b_p$, and the same $b_p$ enters both rows. If residual autocorrelation remains within a participant, the covariance contains more than $\tau_p^2$.

## Adding the crossed word intercept

MALD trials also repeat spoken words. Give word $w$ a deviation $c_w$:

$$
Y_{pwi}=\beta_0+b_p+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi},
$$

where

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),\qquad
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),\qquad
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Two rows that share only a participant have covariance $\tau_p^2$. Two rows that share only a word have covariance $\tau_w^2$. Rows sharing both units have covariance $\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2$ under the model's independence assumptions.

## Fitting the crossed model

The participant, word, and residual variances are estimated by the
[Gaussian mixed model likelihood](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood).
We use REML because the population coefficient structure is fixed here and our
immediate target is the covariance decomposition.

```{r}
#| label: mald-random-intercepts
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ 1 +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

variance_components <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
variance_components[c("grp", "var1", "vcov", "sdcor")]

participant_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "participant_id" &
    is.na(variance_components$var2)
]
item_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "item" &
    is.na(variance_components$var2)
]
residual_variance <- sigma(fit)^2
data.frame(
  participant_variance = participant_variance,
  total_variance = participant_variance + item_variance + residual_variance,
  same_participant_correlation = participant_variance /
    (participant_variance + item_variance + residual_variance)
)
```

The final column is computed from the fitted MALD variance components. It is the model-implied correlation for two responses from the same participant and different words.

We can also reconstruct the covariance for observed trial pairs. The first pair
below shares a participant, the second shares a word, and the third shares
neither. The responses themselves do not enter this covariance calculation;
their identifiers select the fitted components that the pair shares.

```{r}
#| label: check-mald-random-intercept-covariance

same_participant_rows <- mald[
  mald$participant_id == mald$participant_id[[1L]],
]
same_participant_rows <- same_participant_rows[
  !duplicated(same_participant_rows$item),
]
same_participant_rows <- same_participant_rows[seq_len(2L), ]

repeated_word_counts <- table(mald$item)
first_word <- names(repeated_word_counts[repeated_word_counts >= 2L])[[1L]]
same_word_rows <- mald[mald$item == first_word, ]
same_word_rows <- same_word_rows[
  !duplicated(same_word_rows$participant_id),
]
same_word_rows <- same_word_rows[seq_len(2L), ]

different_row <- mald[
  mald$participant_id != same_participant_rows$participant_id[[1L]] &
    mald$item != same_participant_rows$item[[1L]],
][1L, ]

observed_pair_covariances <- data.frame(
  pair = c(
    "same participant, different words",
    "different participants, same word",
    "different participants, different words"
  ),
  first_participant = c(
    same_participant_rows$participant_id[[1L]],
    same_word_rows$participant_id[[1L]],
    same_participant_rows$participant_id[[1L]]
  ),
  second_participant = c(
    same_participant_rows$participant_id[[2L]],
    same_word_rows$participant_id[[2L]],
    different_row$participant_id[[1L]]
  ),
  first_word = c(
    same_participant_rows$item[[1L]],
    same_word_rows$item[[1L]],
    same_participant_rows$item[[1L]]
  ),
  second_word = c(
    same_participant_rows$item[[2L]],
    same_word_rows$item[[2L]],
    different_row$item[[1L]]
  ),
  fitted_covariance = c(
    participant_variance,
    item_variance,
    0
  )
)
observed_pair_covariances
```

The table instantiates the covariance equations with identifiers from retained
MALD trials. It also makes the conditioning statement concrete: once the
participant and word deviations are supplied, the remaining trial residuals are
independent, while averaging over those deviations produces the displayed
covariances.

In `lmer` notation, `(1 | participant_id)` inserts $b_p$ and `(1 | item)` inserts $c_w$. Three trial pairs clarify the implied dependence:

| Pair | Shared component | Model covariance |
|---|---|---:|
| same participant, different words | $b_p$ | $\tau_p^2$ |
| different participants, same word | $c_w$ | $\tau_w^2$ |
| different participants, different words | none | $0$ |

The two grouping terms are crossed because participant and word identifiers recur in many combinations. The formula does not create replication absent from the table; it represents the incidence structure that the table already contains.

## Comparing raw and conditional participant baselines

```{r}
#| label: random-intercept-pooling
raw_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id,
  data = mald,
  FUN = mean
)
names(raw_means)[names(raw_means) == "log_rt"] <- "raw_mean"

participant_modes <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
conditional_means <- data.frame(
  participant_id = rownames(participant_modes),
  conditional_mean =
    fixef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]] + participant_modes[["(Intercept)"]],
  row.names = NULL
)

pooling <- merge(raw_means, conditional_means, by = "participant_id")

ggplot(pooling, aes(x = raw_mean, y = conditional_mean)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey65") +
  geom_point(color = "#1F5A85", size = 1.3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "Raw participant mean log response time",
    y = "Conditional participant mean"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The participant intercept represents persistent response speed differences. Differences in the lexical frequency association require a random slope as well.

## Recap and check

1. Does a participant intercept represent every within-listener dependence? No. Serial dependence or listener-specific slopes require additional structure.
2. Are rows independent after marginalizing over $b_p$? No. Rows sharing the intercept have covariance $\tau_p^2$.

We next convert these fitted covariance components into [intraclass correlations](intraclass-correlation.qmd).
